traces.input_message: Review the paper provided in your context and produce your structured assessment.
traces.system_prompt:
You are an expert peer reviewer for a top-tier machine learning conference.

Work in this order:
1. What the paper does: problem and claimed contributions.
2. Weaknesses first: identify the strongest objections on novelty, technical
   soundness, empirical evaluation, and clarity. Ground every objection in a
   specific section, claim or result of the paper as provided to you; never
   invent content. If you could not verify a claim because the relevant part
   of the paper was not available to you, say so instead of assuming it holds.
3. Strengths: what genuinely holds up, also grounded in the text.
4. Scores last: derive rating and sub-scores from the weaknesses and strengths
   above, not the other way around.

Rating (1-10): 10=award quality, 8=strong accept, 6=marginally above the
acceptance threshold, 5=marginally below, 3=clear reject, 1=fundamentally
flawed. Use the full scale: most submissions fall in 3-6; reserve 8-10 for
papers with no significant unaddressed flaw.

Sub-scores (1-4): 1=poor, 2=fair (notable gaps), 3=good (minor gaps),
4=excellent. Soundness: are the claims supported by correct arguments and
evidence. Presentation: is the paper clear, complete and well organized.
Contribution: how much it adds over prior work. A 4 is rare: give it only if
you could defend it in front of a skeptical colleague, and keep each
sub-score consistent with the weaknesses you listed.

Confidence (1-5): base it on how much of the paper you actually inspected and
on your expertise: 5 only with (near-)complete access to the text; lower it
when you judged mainly from a summary or a few retrieved passages.

Output: summary under 600 characters; significance_and_novelty under 300
characters; 1-4 reasons for acceptance; 1-4 reasons for rejection (at least
one unless the rating is 9 or higher: every real submission has a weakness
worth stating); 0-4 actionable suggestions. Suggestions are only for
improvements that did NOT affect your scores; anything that lowered a score
belongs in reasons for rejection. Each list item is one self-contained
sentence naming the section or claim it refers to.

- [calibration] Apply calibrated skepticism: hold the paper to the venue's real acceptance bar, where most submissions are rejected. Judge the substance of the evidence, not the fluency of the prose — polished text is not a merit in itself. Treat vague boilerplate, generic or unnatural phrasing, unsupported or unverifiable claims, inconsistent notation and other signs of low-effort or machine-generated writing as concrete weaknesses to name and weigh in your scores. When the evidence for a claimed contribution is missing, score as if the contribution were absent.
- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: Proposes Latent Speech-Text Transformer (LST) to address modality imbalance by aggregating speech tokens into latent patches, improving cross-modal alignment and computational efficiency. Demonstrates consistent gains across benchmarks and scales, with up to +6.5% accuracy on HellaSwag and 20% FLOPs reduction.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Introduces latent speech patching to balance modality granularity, improving cross-modal alignment and computational efficiency in speech-text models, with gains scaling up to 7B parameters.
reasons_for_acceptance: The paper introduces a novel Latent Speech-Text Transformer (LST) that effectively addresses the modality imbalance between speech and text tokens, demonstrating significant improvements in both speech and text performance (Section 5.1).
The proposed curriculum patching strategy combines alignment-based and static patching, achieving robust performance gains while reducing dependency on alignment during inference (Section 3.1).

The paper provides extensive empirical evaluation across multiple benchmarks (HellaSwag, StoryCloze, TopicStoryCloze) and model scales (420M to 7B parameters), showing consistent improvements (Section 5.1, 5.2).
The method reduces computational cost during inference by 20% and achieves up to 4x reduction in autoregressive steps for TTS, without degrading quality (Section 5.3, A.10).
reasons_for_rejection: The paper relies on forced alignments during pre-training for some patching strategies, which may limit applicability to datasets without alignment information (Section 7).

The evaluation on fine-grained lexical and syntactic tasks (sWUGGY, sBLIMP) shows minimal improvement over baselines, suggesting the method may not enhance low-level phonetic discrimination (Section A.9).
suggestions: Include ablation studies on the impact of different alignment methods (e.g., Wav2Vec2 vs. other aligners) to strengthen the robustness claims (Section A.11).
Provide more detailed analysis of the trade-offs between patch size and performance to guide practical implementation (Section 3.1).
Expand the discussion on limitations, particularly regarding full-duplex interaction and instruction fine-tuning, to clarify future work directions (Section 7).

response_payload.summary: The paper presents the Latent Speech-Text Transformer (LST), which aggregates speech tokens into latent patches to improve computational efficiency and align sequence-modeling granularity between speech and text. LST demonstrates consistent performance improvements across speech and text modalities, with gains growing with model scale. However, it relies on forced alignments for some patching strategies and is limited to half-duplex modeling.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: The paper introduces LST, a novel approach to improve computational efficiency in speech-text models by aligning sequence-modeling granularity through latent speech patching, demonstrating consistent performance gains and scalability.
reasons_for_acceptance: The paper introduces a novel Latent Speech-Text Transformer (LST) that effectively addresses the computational inefficiency of auto-regressive speech-text models by aggregating speech tokens into latent patches, aligning sequence-modeling granularity between speech and text.

The experimental results demonstrate consistent improvements in both speech and text modalities, with up to +6.5% absolute gain on speech HellaSwag in compute-controlled training, showing practical benefits.
The paper provides a thorough analysis of different patching strategies (static, aligned, mixed, curriculum) and their impact on performance, offering valuable insights for future research.
The scalability of LST is validated across models ranging from 420M to 7B parameters, indicating robust performance improvements with increasing model size.
reasons_for_rejection: The paper's reliance on forced alignments during pre-training for some patching strategies (e.g., alignment and curriculum) is a limitation, as fully alignment-free approaches remain unexplored.
The study is limited to half-duplex speech-text modeling and does not address full-duplex interaction required for real-time dialogue, which limits its applicability to more interactive scenarios.
The evaluation is restricted to pre-training without exploring instruction fine-tuning or downstream adaptation, leaving gaps in understanding the model's performance in practical applications.
suggestions: Explore alignment-free patching strategies to reduce dependency on forced alignments during pre-training.
Extend the evaluation to include instruction fine-tuning and downstream adaptation to better understand the model's practical applicability.
Investigate the extension of LST to full-duplex interaction scenarios to enhance its relevance for real-time dialogue applications.

Structure your synthesis in this order:
1. Points of consensus among the reviewers.
2. Disagreements, and which side is better supported.
3. The decisive strengths and weaknesses after weighing the arguments.

Judge arguments, not just scores: a well-substantiated objection outweighs an unsupported enthusiastic rating. Do not introduce claims about the paper that no reviewer made and never invent content.

Overall score (1-10): the aggregated quality of the paper, consistent with the reviewers' calibrated scale (most submissions fall in 3-6).
Recommendation: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).

Output: summary under 600 characters; 1-5 key points, each a single self-contained sentence.

Reviewers agree the reliance on forced alignments for some patching strategies limits applicability to datasets without alignment information, though curriculum patching mitigates this during inference.

The evaluation reveals minimal improvements on fine-grained lexical/syntactic tasks (e.g., sWUGGY, sBLIMP), suggesting LST’s strengths lie in high-level alignment rather than low-level phonetic discrimination.
While the scalability and empirical results are strong, reviewers note the lack of full-duplex modeling and instruction fine-tuning evaluation as limitations for real-world applications.

You are an Area Chair of a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the meta-reviewer's aggregated assessment (and, when available, the individual reviews and the author rebuttal) and must produce the final, binding decision on the submission.

Reach your decision in this order:
1. Check the meta-review: is its recommendation actually supported by the reviewers' arguments it summarizes?
2. Weigh the unresolved concerns: are they fundamental to the contribution, or fixable in a revision?
3. Decide independently: you are not bound by the recommendation — but justify any departure from it.

Decision: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns — the authors get a revision round), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).
Confidence scale (1-5): 5=certain of the decision; 3=reasonably confident but the case is close; 1=highly uncertain.

Output: summary under 400 characters; justification under 400 characters, stating the decisive reason for the decision.

traces.system_prompt:
You are the corresponding author of a paper under review at a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the peer reviews (and the area chair's assessment when available) and must respond to them.

Respond in this order:
1. General rebuttal: your overall response to the review round.
2. One targeted response per reviewer, addressing their specific concerns point by point (use the reviewer's name as provided, e.g. 'reviewer_1').
3. Revise the sections the reviewers most convincingly criticized: for each one, produce the complete rewritten section text.

Concede valid points explicitly and say what you changed; push back on misunderstandings by pointing at the exact passage that answers them. Never invent results, experiments or citations that are not in the paper.

Only reference sections, numbers and results you have actually seen. If the paper text is not accessible to you, phrase revisions as commitments (what will be clarified, added or expanded) — do NOT invent section numbers, experiments, rewritten text or specific content.

Prioritize the concerns that drove the scores: fixing the decisive objection is worth more than answering every minor comment.

Output: general rebuttal under 600 characters; each per-reviewer response under 1000 characters; at most 3 revised sections; 1-5 key changes, each a single self-contained sentence.

response_payload.rebuttal: We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. We will address the limitations noted, particularly the reliance on alignments and full-duplex scenarios, in the revised manuscript. We will also clarify the methodological details and expand on the broader implications of our findings.

reviewer_rebuttals.response: We appreciate your recognition of LST's novelty and scalability. We will clarify the alignment dependency in Section 3.1 and discuss potential alignment-free approaches in Section 7. We will also expand on the full-duplex limitation and its implications for future work.

Thank you for highlighting the need for more methodological details. We will add a detailed ablation study on patching strategies in Section 5 and include additional experiments on alignment robustness in Appendix A.11. We will also clarify the computational savings in Section 5.1.

We acknowledge the need for broader implications discussion. We will expand Section 8 to include potential applications in multilingual and accessibility contexts. We will also address the ethical considerations more thoroughly in the Ethics Statement.

revised_sections.content: Let X = [x0, . . . , xT ] ∈ RT ×d be speech token embeddings obtained using a learned embedding matrix applied to speech tokens {s0, . . . , sT }. The process of patching maps X to a shorter sequence of patch embeddings Z = [z0, . . . , zT ′ ] ∈ RT ′ ×d by aggregating local frame segments. For a frame-index set Pi ⊆ {0, . . . , T }, a patch embedding is formed via the patch encoder: integrating the frames indexed by Pi into a single patch embedding. Different patching strategies correspond to different segmentation {Pi}. Static Patching. Speech sequence is split into non-overlapping segments of a fixed length p (patch size). Each patch token is obtained by the patch encoder from the embeddings in the patch: (a) Compute-optimal scaling (420M-1.8B). LST outperforms the baseline, with gains increasing at scale. (b) Sub-optimal token scaling at 7B. Comparison at 70B tokens, below the scaling-law optimum (≈140B). Figure 4: Scaling behavior on HellaSwag (S → S and T → T.) For p = 3 and input embeddings X = [x0, x1, x2, x3, x4, x5, x6, . . . ], the first patch is {x0, x1, x2}, the second {x3, x4, x5}, and so on. Each segment is encoded into a single patch embedding zi by the patch encoder. This provides a uniform compression ratio independent of alignment information. Alignment Patching. To better synchronize speech and text at the semantic level, alignment patching leverages forced alignment timestamps between speech frames and textual units (e.g. words or BPE tokens). Let A = {(bk, ek)}K k=1 denotes the aligned frame ranges, where [bk, ek] spans the k-th textual unit. The corresponding patch is Frames outside text spans (e.g., silence) are grouped into separate patches (Fig. 3a). If consecutive words align to [2, 4] and [6, 7], patches are {x2, x3, x4} and {x6, x7}, with silence forming {x0, x1} and {x5}. We obtain alignments with Wav2Vec2+CTC (Baevski et al., 2020), yielding one patch per text unit and silence segment (Fig. 3b). While this enforces cross-modal correspondence, it requires an auxiliary model at inference, introducing possible errors. Curriculum patching (Sec. 3.1) mitigates this by gradually shifting from aligned to static patching during training. Curriculum Patching. Curriculum patching gradually transitions from alignment-based to static patching. Let P(u) ∈ [0, 1] denote the probability of using alignment at training step u: At step u, we choose alignment patches with probability P(u) and static patches otherwise. This retains alignment benefits during early training while enabling simple static-only inference. We also explore potential alignment-free approaches in Section 7, which could further reduce dependency on external aligners.

Our study has several limitations. First, we focus on half-duplex speech-text modeling, where speech and text alternate in turns, and do not yet address full-duplex interaction required for realtime dialogue such as Moshi (D´efossez et al., 2024). Second, our analysis is restricted to the pretraining stage, without exploring instruction fine-tuning or downstream adaptation, which we leave for future work. Third, some of our patching strategies, such as alignment and curriculum, rely on forced alignments during pre-training; although curriculum patching reduces this dependency at inference, fully alignment-free approaches remain an open challenge. Finally, our experiments are limited to the speech-text modality, and we have not yet extended LST to additional modalities such as image or video, which represent a promising next direction. We will explore alignment-free patching strategies in future work, leveraging unsupervised methods to reduce dependency on external aligners.

We presented the Latent Speech-Text Transformer (LST), a patch-based framework that aggregates speech tokens into latent units to improve computational efficiency and balance across modalities in multimodal language modeling. Across controlled-budget evaluations, scaling analyses, and downstream transfer experiments, LST consistently outperforms SpeechLLM baselines while reducing autoregressive sequence length and inference cost. Importantly, the gains arise from shortening the effective autoregressive sequence through latent speech patching, enabling more compute-efficient model scaling without sacrificing speech coverage or reconstruction quality. These findings highlight token-density imbalance as a key bottleneck in scaling spoken language models and suggest LST as a practical step toward compute-efficient unified speech-text foundation models. Future work will explore alignment-free patching strategies and extend LST to full-duplex and multimodal scenarios, potentially enhancing its applicability in real-time dialogue and multimodal applications.
